1.title: Backends, Remote State and State Locking
1.text: Welcome to Module thirteen: Backends, Remote State and State Locking. It covers the exam area six. Terraform state management. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. six A Describe the local backend. six B Describe state locking. six C Configure remote state using the backend block. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: six. Terraform state management. Exam format: a one-hour online-proctored multiple-choice exam on Terraform one point one two. Validated against: the official Terraform Associate version oh oh four exam objectives.

1.title: What a backend is
1.text: What a backend is. A backend defines where Terraform stores its state and how operations run.

1.title: What a backend is, continued
1.text: What a backend is. The figure shows this: The local backend stores state on disk; a remote backend stores it in shared storage with locking.

1.title: What a backend is, continued
1.text: What a backend is. local (the default). A file terraform dot tfstate in the working directory (path can be changed). Remote (for example S three, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, Consul, a database). Shared storage outside your machine. H C P Terraform (the cloud block). H C P Terraform workspaces (Module sixteen).

1.title: The local backend
1.text: The local backend. Default. Used when no backend is configured. File. terraform dot tfstate, and terraform dot tfstate dot backup for the previous version. Locking. Locks the file while an operation runs (system file locking). Limits. Not shared; no encryption or versioning; unsuitable for teams. Configure path. backend local path... Exam tip: The local backend is the default and stores terraform dot tfstate next to your configuration. It is fine for learning and bad for teams.

1.title: Configuring remote state with the backend block
1.text: Configuring remote state with the backend block. The backend block is nested in the terraform block. A configuration has at most one backend. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Configuring remote state with the backend block, continued
1.text: Configuring remote state with the backend block. No variables or references. Backend arguments must be literal values; use partial configuration ( terraform init -backend config... ) or environment variables for the rest. Credentials. Supply them outside the file (environment variables, instance roles). After adding or changing a backend. Run terraform init; Terraform offers to migrate the state ( -migrate state ); -reconfigure ignores the old settings. Benefits. Sharing, locking, encryption, versioning, access control. Reading another configuration's state: the terraform remote state data source reads the root-module outputs of another state.

1.title: Configuring remote state with the backend block, continued
1.text: Configuring remote state with the backend block. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: Backend settings cannot use variables. terraform remote state exposes only the root outputs of the other configuration.

1.title: State locking
1.text: State locking. State locking prevents two operations from writing the state at the same time, which could corrupt it. When it locks. During operations that could write state: plan, apply, destroy and some state commands. Automatic. On by default where the backend supports it. Backend support. Most remote backends (for example S three with a lock file, Azure, Google Cloud Storage); not every backend. -lock false. Turns locking off (dangerous). -lock timeout D U R A T I O N. Wait for a lock to be released instead of failing at once. terraform force unlock L O C K I D. Releases a stuck lock (use only if no run is active). Exam tip: Locking prevents concurrent state changes. force unlock is for a stuck lock only, and -lock false is rarely a good idea.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A configuration has no backend block. Where is the state stored? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: In a file named terraform.tfstate in the working directory. Without a backend block the local backend stores terraform.tfstate in the working directory.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A team wants shared, encrypted, locked state. What should they configure? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A remote backend in the terraform block. A remote backend stores state in shared storage and supports locking.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Can the arguments of a backend block use input variables? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: No, they must be literal values or supplied another way. Backend settings cannot use variables or references; use partial configuration or environment variables.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. What is the purpose of state locking? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: To prevent concurrent operations from corrupting the state. Locking stops two operations from writing the state at the same time.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A run crashed and left a lock behind. No one else is running Terraform. What can be used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: terraform force-unlock with the lock I D. force-unlock releases a stuck lock, and should only be used when no run is active.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. What does the terraform remote state data source provide? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: The root module outputs of another configuration's state. It reads the root-module outputs stored in another state.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the default backend? Answer: The local backend. Question two. Where is the backend block written? Answer: Inside the terraform block. Question three. Can backend arguments use variables? Answer: No.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What does state locking prevent? Answer: Concurrent changes that corrupt the state. Question five. Which command releases a stuck lock? Answer: terraform force-unlock. Question six. What happens after changing the backend? Answer: Run terraform init; Terraform can migrate the state.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Backends: local (default, terraform.tfstate), remote (S three, Azure, G C S, Consul), H C P Terraform (cloud block). Backend block: in the terraform block; one only; literal values; init after changes. Remote state: sharing, locking, encryption, versioning; terraform remote state reads outputs. Locking: automatic where supported; -lock equals false, -lock-timeout, force-unlock.
